title: How a sentence changes its starting point while the participants and the underlying event remain exactly the same
subtitle: See what English passive voice changes, and what it leaves intact.
subject: Language · English grammar
limits: This lesson uses ordinary past-simple transitive clauses. It does not cover every passive construction. Sentence topic is not the same as the only important or new information; context and stress also affect focus.
hook: You are writing about a bicycle. Starting with the bicycle keeps it as the thread of the story, even when somebody else does the work.

steps.title: Keep the participants and their event roles distinct from the subject and the first words of the sentence
steps.say:
In our example, Maya does the repairing and the bicycle is affected. Those are roles in the event. In the active sentence, Maya is also the grammatical subject.

Switch to passive. The bicycle becomes the subject. Maya is still the doer.
steps.sayText: In our example, Maya does the repairing and the bicycle is affected. Those are roles in the event. In the active sentence, Maya is also the grammatical subject.Switch to passive. The bicycle becomes the subject. Maya is still the doer.
steps.lookFor: the coloured roles stay put while the sentence starts with a different participant
steps.note: Grammatical subject and doer are different roles.

alts.label: Follow the event
alts.say: Imagine watching the repair with the sound off. Changing the sentence cannot change the person holding the tools.

ask.q: In 'The bicycle was repaired by Maya', who does the repairing?
ask.why: Maya remains the doer. The bicycle is the passive subject and the affected thing.

steps.figureLabel: In a repair, Maya is the doer and the bicycle is affected. The selected active sentence is: Maya repaired the bicycle. The doer is named.

steps.title: Change the sentence, not the event
steps.say: These past-simple passives use was + past participle: was repaired, or was painted. A by-phrase can name the doer.
steps.sayText: These past-simple passives use was + past participle: was repaired, or was painted. A by-phrase can name the doer.
steps.note: Affected thing + was + past participle, with an optional by-phrase.

ask.q: Which is the passive of 'The team painted the gate'?
ask.why: 'Was painted' is passive. Merely reversing the names changes who did what.
ask.answerText: The gate was painted by the team.

steps.figureLabel: In a repair, Maya is the doer and the bicycle is affected. The selected passive sentence is: The bicycle was repaired by Maya. The doer is named.

state.label: a repair
state.sentence: The bicycle was repaired by Maya.

steps.answerText: The gate was painted by the team.

steps.title: Omitting the doer loses some information
steps.say:
'The bicycle was repaired' leaves the doer unstated. It can suit a story about the bicycle when who repaired it is unknown, obvious or unimportant.

That shorter sentence does not tell its reader that Maya did it.

steps.note: Unstated is not the same as nonexistent.

ask.q: Does 'The bicycle was repaired' identify Maya as the doer?
ask.why: The event has a doer, but the sentence does not identify them. Omission is not evidence that nobody acted.

ask.q: How can two sentences describe the same event but start differently?
